task_row_model.query: In Python, what's the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy for nested lists? Show a short example where modifying a nested element affects the original list and one where it doesn't.

documents.content: Assigning one list variable to another simply binds a new name to the same list object; no copy is made. To create a new top-level list that shares the same elements, you can use slicing (lst[:] ) or the list.copy() method; both return a new list object whose items are references to the same contained objects. For example, a shallow copy will give you an independent outer list, but if the elements themselves are mutable objects like sublists, they remain shared between the original and the copy.

List comprehensions and generator expressions are concise ways to build sequences and can sometimes be used instead of manual loops for efficiency. A list comprehension evaluates immediately and returns a full list, while a generator expression yields values lazily. For large data sets, generators save memory. This topic focuses on creation and iteration patterns, not on object copying semantics or reference sharing between nested mutable structures.

Conceptually, a shallow copy duplicates only the container object and not the nested objects within it: references to inner objects are copied, not the objects themselves. A deep copy recursively copies the container and all objects reachable from it, producing entirely separate structures. With nested lists, a shallow copy means inner lists are still the same objects, so mutating an inner list affects both structures, whereas a deep copy isolates them. The precise mechanism in code depends on language libraries and how special methods are implemented for custom classes.

In Python, a shallow copy makes a new outer list but keeps references to the same inner objects; a deep copy duplicates inner objects as well. Example: original = [[1], [2]]; shallow = original.copy(); shallow[0].append(99) will modify original to [[1, 99], [2]] because shallow[0] and original[0] reference the same sublist. In contrast, using copy.deepcopy from the copy module creates independent inner lists: import copy; deep = copy.deepcopy(original); deep[0].append(99) leaves original unchanged. Reassigning a top-level element (shallow[0] = [42]) does not affect the original outer list.

In Java, cloning an object via the Cloneable interface often performs a shallow copy unless override methods implement deep cloning. Developers commonly implement deep copy by manually cloning fields or using serialization libraries to produce a new object graph. C++ uses copy constructors and assignment operators to control copying behavior; smart pointers and explicit cloning patterns help manage ownership and avoid shared mutable state. These language-specific patterns are relevant when porting algorithms, but differ in syntax and standard library support compared to Python's copy semantics.
